newsitem.title: INDIA: Legal net tightens around India's Rao.
newsitem.headline: Legal net tightens around India's Rao.

text.p: Pressure mounted on former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao to relinquish his last major political post on Thursday as he prepared for a second appearance before a trial judge.
Federal police indicted Rao in a vote-buying case on Wednesday, hours after he appeared in a special courtroom in a separate criminal forgery case.
The indictment piled pressure on Rao to step down as head of the Congress party's parliamentary delegation, newspapers said.

Rao, who resigned as prime minister in May after Congress was defeated in general polls, quit as Congress party leader in September after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court in a third criminal case, involving alleged cheating.

But he has remained head of the Congress Parliamentary Party (CPP) and retains influence over India's 13-party United Front (UF) coalition, which depends on Congress's backing to survive a challenge from right-wing Hindu nationalists.

The Asian Age said Rao was likely to step down as CPP leader. Referring to the indictment in the 1993 vote-buying case, the newspaper said "it was unlikely that he would retain the post now that he was charge-sheeted in a fresh case".
The Observer said the fresh indictment had "come as a shot in the arm for the Rao-detractors within the party, while giving anxious moments to the United Front coalition government".
The newspaper said Rao's woes "may precipitate a review of the Congress-UF relationship in the backdrop of the persistent demand perpetuated by Rao opponents".
If Rao stepped down as CPP leader, pressure could mount on Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda to include Congress members in his cabinet, the Observer said.
But such a move would be contested by left-wing parties in the government coalition which have strained ties with Congress.

On Wednesday, Rao became the first former or serving prime minister to appear in court on criminal charges. Rao and five others have been charged with trying to defame a rival politician in 1989 by using forged bank documents.
His lawyer, R.K. Anand, told the chief metropolitan magistrate that Rao was not named in the original complaint filed with police in 1990, and that the case against his client was "fabricated".
Hours after Rao left the trial hearing, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) indicted the former prime minister and six others in the vote-buying case.
The CBI said it charged Rao with conspiring to pay legislators from a regional party $100,000 to vote against a 1993 no-confidence motion, which Congress narrowly won.
Rao and the other Congress leaders have denied any wrongdoing.

The bail hearing in the forgery case was set to resume at 10 a.m. (0430 GMT) on Thursday, and Anand said Rao would attend. It was not known when the judge would rule on Rao's request for an extension of bail protection against arrest, which expires on November 6.
